#5097. Scaramucci Says JPMorgan Could Spend Up to $1 Billion on Its Bitcoin Business

JPMorgan may have to spend between $500 million and $1 billion to build out its Bitcoin business, according to SkyBridge Capital's Anthony Scaramucci.

It is JPMorgan's willingness to spend money serving Bitcoin clients that tells us more about its plans than CEO Jamie Dimon calling the cryptocurrency a "pet rock."

Scaramucci also claimed that a research note circulating within JPMorgan's private bank recommended allocating 10% of a portfolio to Bitcoin, describing it as potentially the most undervalued asset of the next decade.

The American financier did not provide a timeline for the spending estimate. Neither the estimate nor the research note could be independently verified through publicly available JPMorgan documents.

"Know the difference between what people say and what they do with their money," Scaramucci wrote on X.

Scaramucci was referring to what it might cost JPMorgan to develop a business serving Bitcoin clients.

The 10% allocation recommendation, meanwhile, concerns how much of a client's portfolio should be invested in Bitcoin.

If you have a $1 million portfolio, that would mean allocating $100,000 to Bitcoin.

It doesn't mean JPMorgan is buying Bitcoin and adding it to its own balance sheet.

There is a specific example of what JPMorgan already offers in a securities filing dated Nov. 24.

The filing covers $300,000 worth of notes linked to BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF, priced by JPMorgan's financing subsidiary.

Someone who invests $1,000 in these notes could receive $1,300 if the ETF closes at or above its initial price on the observation date in November 2027.

Scaramucci suggested that Dimon has regulators in mind when he publicly criticizes Bitcoin.

"He's a smart guy. He knows he has to go before regulators and say the right things," Scaramucci said.

In a CNBC interview at Davos in January 2024, Dimon described Bitcoin as a "pet rock."

At JPMorgan's investor day in May 2025, Dimon raised concerns about leverage and illicit activity involving Bitcoin.

However, he also made it clear that customers could buy Bitcoin and see their holdings reflected on JPMorgan statements. At the time, he said the bank would leave custody to third parties.

"I defend your right to buy Bitcoin," Dimon said.

#5096. How Coldcard’s $112 million Bitcoin exploit slipped past 15 security reviews

Independent researchers repeatedly examined Coldcard's firmware without discovering the vulnerability that ultimately enabled widespread Bitcoin theft.

A security flaw in Coldcard's Bitcoin hardware wallets went undetected for more than five years despite at least 15 independent security research and review efforts.

Coinkite, the wallet's manufacturer, published its postmortem on Nov. 24, detailing how a firmware defect introduced in March 2021 weakened the recovery phrases generated by its devices, enabling attackers to steal customers' Bitcoin without accessing their hardware wallets.

An Aug. 14 analysis by Galaxy Research identified with high confidence 1,778.84 BTC, worth $112.7 million at the time, stolen from more than 8,600 addresses. Galaxy estimated that losses could reach 2,417 BTC, or $153 million, if additional suspected thefts were confirmed.

Coinkite said it had matched approximately 300 loss-related support tickets to 236 customer accounts, representing about 0.2% of its estimated user base. However, the company acknowledged that the actual number of affected customers was likely higher.

The vulnerability originated from a firmware configuration error that caused Coldcard devices to generate recovery phrases using a weaker software-based random number generator instead of the intended hardware component.

The devices continued producing apparently valid recovery phrases, allowing the defect to escape routine security and functionality tests.

Coinkite's postmortem estimates that the defect substantially reduced the randomness protecting recovery phrases across five Coldcard models, including the Mk2, Mk3, Mk4, Mk5 and Q.

Attackers exploited that weakness to reconstruct private keys offline and transfer Bitcoin from affected wallets.

Between 2021 and 2026, Coldcard underwent at least 15 independent security research and review efforts, including two paid third-party product reviews. Its publicly available firmware repository also had 54 contributors.

One commissioned review in March 2022 specifically examined random-number generation and related security measures without discovering the defect.

More recently, independent security researcher Rob Hamilton used OpenAI's Cybersecurity Harness to examine Coldcard's firmware between May 1 and June 26.

The AI-assisted review generated 85 potential security findings, several of which prompted fixes, but failed to identify the seed-generation vulnerability.

A separate June 17 review by security researcher Nick Farrow also examined weak random-number generation and concluded that the relevant implementation was sound.

Coinkite attributed these failures to a gap in its verification process. Existing checks established that the hardware random-number generator was present in the firmware but failed to confirm whether the software actually used it to create recovery phrases.

The company identified the defect on July 30, following the first reported thefts, and released corrected firmware the following day.

Security firm Keylabs subsequently verified the fix across four firmware releases for Coldcard's Mk5 and Q wallets.

Coinkite has also introduced additional safeguards that combine user-provided randomness with multiple hardware sources when generating new recovery phrases.

However, these changes cannot strengthen recovery phrases created using the defective firmware, leaving previously affected wallets exposed even after their owners install the latest updates.

Keylabs traced the seed-generation fix to four signed releases. Owners keeping a wallet still need to know how its original recovery phrase was created.

Coinkite advises moving funds to a fresh wallet if the original seed was affected or its origin is unclear.

The audit covers the seed-generation fix on the four listed standard releases. Coinkite’s migration guide details the qualifying dice exception and secure external imports.

The upper path follows the scope in Keylabs’ October 15 report. The lower path follows Coinkite’s affected-seed migration guidance.

The audit covers the seed-generation fix on the four listed standard releases. Coinkite’s migration guide details the qualifying dice exception and secure external imports.

Coinkite said wallets using securely generated external recovery phrases were unaffected. Owners who incorporated at least 50 fair, independent and private dice rolls during their original wallet setup also remained protected if they followed the prescribed procedure.

The company advises other affected users to generate new recovery phrases using verified firmware and transfer their Bitcoin to the resulting wallets.

Meanwhile, law enforcement continues investigating the thefts, and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security has opened a separate case.

Coinkite has appealed to whoever controls the stolen Bitcoin to return the funds. Nearly four months after the exploit, however, the company has yet to decide whether it will compensate affected customers.

#5094. Bitcoin Has Become Boring, Finally

Bitcoin isn't a shiny new technology any more, it is established, and it is here to stay.

The 2019 Lightning conference in Berlin was lit: five hundred “cypherpunks” getting each other high on visions of a future with peer-to-peer electronic cash. Attending a bitcoin conference back in the day felt like being a teenager at a friend’s party while their parents were out of town. It was exciting and new. The feeling was the opposite of FOMO: something big was happening, we were on the inside, and the rest of the world was going to envy us. It was the kind of party that you could only have when the adults weren’t looking. Whenever someone bought a beer (with bitcoin), everyone would hoot and holler and record it on their phones for Instagram/Twitter (it was still called Twitter).

Lightning was the bleeding edge. We called it “the Lightning Network” (capitalized, if you please), and talking about it felt like talking about string theory: something so far out you’re not even sure it’s real. I spent a lot of time invoking the abacus.

Those are the times some of us remember fondly and keep trying to relive at bitcoin conferences today. That’s why we engage in rituals like drone shows, Satoshi Rockamoto sets, beefsteak dinners, and video game tournaments for sats, but it’s not the same. The ratio of bitcoin OG speakers to suits is shifting. Many event rooms are half empty, and the halls and meeting rooms are full of people negotiating cap tables and profit-sharing splits.

The adults haven’t shut the party down, but they have crashed it, and it kinda feels like their party now. The most exciting thing I noticed at the last bitcoin conference I attended was that nothing exciting happened.

The road to boring is seldom smooth. Technological innovation benefits from passion and bold ideas. People work harder on a project when they feel strongly about it and identify closely with like-minded collaborators. That’s where tech subcultures, their rituals, and their dogmas come from. But such passion and tribalism feed conflict, at least for a while until the tech goes mainstream, and normies, who couldn’t care less about subculture squabbles, take over.

This progression from an exciting new technology that inspires strong emotions to a humdrum utility is not unusual. World-changing innovations often (always?) start with a committed subculture that identifies fiercely with their weird tech before the mainstream adopts it and soon expects it. In fact, this trajectory has become the standard doctrine of tech marketing. For example, in the early days of the internet, early adopters wrote a Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace, picking a fight with states and corporations despite having nothing to back it up but chatrooms and dreams.

One case that resembles the early days of bitcoin was the war of the currents between high-voltage AC current and low-voltage DC current in the 1880s-1890s. Both featured big personalities stunning audiences with flashy demos at conferences. Edison and Westinghouse wowed crowds with their lightbulbs that made artificial light, just like bitcoiners in 2019 wowed YouTube by buying beer with bitcoin. And both cases featured rabid subcultures that accused each other of putting the future of the technology, if not of humanity, at stake. In the 1880s, the issue was whether AC was more deadly to humans and animals than DC; in the 2010s it was whether limiting the size of bitcoin’s blocks to 1MB would perpetuate monetary servitude forever.

In both cases, there were devoted subcultures whose disagreements helped the technology to mature before the tech crossed the chasm of exoticism to become the new, boring normal. Both are now largely managed by experts on pragmatic principles, not passionate conviction. Conferences went from spectacular showcases for technological miracles to sedate affairs where professionals debate and agree on industry standards. Pragmatism and consensus replaced ideology and dissent. In both instances things got boring, and boring was actually better.

Bitcoin is getting boring, although what that means and how it’s come to be that way depends on your point of view. As always, where you stand depends on where you sit.

Generally speaking, there are two broad points of view on what bitcoin is and is for. And though they started in different places, they’re both coming to a common conclusion: bitcoin is more boring than ever. So let’s review these two points of view, how they view bitcoin now, and why both would agree that the status quo is now so awfully, wonderfully boring.

The basic existential question that defined bitcoin’s first decade is settled: bitcoin is not a scam, and it’s not going away. That status is stable largely because bitcoin is now too big to fail, with a market cap exceeding a trillion dollars.

Much of this scale is thanks to the millions of people who want to own bitcoin as part of their savings, but not necessarily to trade and circulate it. In other words, they see bitcoin as a better form of gold, not cash. These savers want to integrate bitcoin into their fiat portfolio, just like any other asset. They aren’t terribly concerned about bitcoin’s status as a medium of exchange so long as it becomes firmly established as a viable, tradable commodity.

People investing in bitcoin are happy when the number goes up, and it generally does (you might have to zoom out on the price graph a bit, depending on the week). Bitcoin used to be a rollercoaster; now it’s more of a hike. The ups and downs still happen, but they’re gentler and a bit more predictable. How boring.

Bitcoin’s price started to settle down as mainstream finance started growing more comfortable with it as an asset. Whereas conventional finance used to want governments to shut bitcoin down, there is now about $100B worth of bitcoin held in ETFs and traded on ordinary equity markets. Major banks used to shun bitcoin, and now they accept it as collateral. Bitcoin is a regular feature in corporate treasuries, and some companies exist just to hold bitcoin. Strategy is worth about $55B on the open market, and it holds about $63B worth of bitcoin, so the entire company is a discounted bitcoin wallet. Bitcoin is also a regular feature in retirement accounts, pension allocations, and sovereign wealth funds. Thinking of bitcoin as another kind of asset ripe for institutional and retail investors now makes a lot of sense, because that’s what it is.

Why are these canny investors bored? It seems that all the exciting developments leading to bitcoin becoming a valuable asset have already happened. If the goal was integration into the world of conventional finance, it has incontrovertibly been achieved. You can’t YOLO on bitcoin any more than you can YOLO on gold. The milestones are all in the history section of the Wikipedia page, not on the roadmap.

People who wanted bitcoin to become a tradable asset are bored because mainstream finance has effectively tamed bitcoin. It is easily tradable, and its trading volumes are remarkable. It is digital gold, just with a slightly steeper curve and a little more volatility, which is exactly what these folks always wanted.

The main alternative to seeing bitcoin as a mainstream investment asset is to view it as monetary dynamite to ignite a revolution. People subscribing to this point of view wanted bitcoin to blossom into a system of peer-to-peer electronic cash that would first operate in parallel to the mainstream monetary system before supplanting it. These radicals wanted to see the banks collapse, not accept bitcoin as collateral. It was monetary insurrection, not incremental change.

This radical point of view is still around, but the wind has gone out of its combative sails for a few reasons.

First, there has been a generational shift. Many of the people who were pushing the revolutionary vision of bitcoin in their 20s fifteen years ago have moved on. Some got rich and retired or started to see and use bitcoin more as a tradable asset. For others, bitcoin never achieved the success they dreamt of, but it was successful enough that fighting for its future no longer felt necessary.

Second, AI is the new cool kid on the tech block. Instead of building vending machines for beer that accept bitcoin, enthusiasts who want to hack the system are now decompiling games with AI. No VC will waste a second on a pitch deck that doesn’t have AI on at least half of the slides. Miners are turning their server stacks and power contracts into AI data centers. Curious engineers have a new, much bigger toy to play with.

Third, mainstream bitcoin fans on Wall Street simply consume too much bandwidth. Not surprisingly, banks, publicly traded companies, and financial institutions with billions in their pockets are dominating panels at conferences and supplying the talking heads for financial news shows. They want to discuss topics like volatility and discount rates instead of personal sovereignty and individual financial freedom. Fighting against the system is not a narrative they can sell while representing the interests of that very system.

Fourth, bitcoin usage has moved past the radical mantras and progressed in a different direction. The dream of bitcoin becoming the standard payment medium in a circular economy where everyone buys coffee with bitcoin (why is it always coffee?) is starting to feel like an alternative history in a parallel universe.

A circular economy is simply not the role in society bitcoin has grown into. Instead of everyday payments, bitcoin is the medium of global value transfer. It has evolved into a technology to move real money across borders as remittances, into a settlement layer between various crypto assets, and into a store of value that people constantly buy, sell, and trade. It’s become a valuable network of rails that even stablecoins are happy to use.

Fixating on coffee purchases obscures the remarkable scale bitcoin has achieved. Somewhere between $1.6 and $4.1 trillion was settled on-chain between Q1 and Q3 2026 (depending on how you count). PayPal processed $1.79 trillion in all of 2025. The average payment on PayPal is about $70. The average bitcoin transaction (using the strict counting method) is $10,000. With bitcoin moving trillions in value, we can stop worrying about coffee.

Bitcoin may not have cornered retail payments, but it’s a mature and highly liquid asset. It’s an industry unto itself. It has found its place in the economy, and it’s thriving. Despite the lack of revolutionary fireworks, bitcoin is changing mainstream finance by opening new possibilities and financially enfranchising new user groups. That’s still worth celebrating.

You know what’s really boring? Electricity infrastructure. You know what no one can live without despite how boring it is? Electricity infrastructure.

When revolutionary technologies fade into the background of everyday life, when people use them constantly without thinking about them, they become boring, and they become essential. Buying a beer with Lightning is no longer exciting because we can now expect that it will just work without fanfare. Being able to say “it will just work” sounds boring, but it’s a clear sign of triumph.

Bitcoiners and builders need to adjust to this beautiful, boring reality. We can stop annoying our neighbors with orange pills. It’s about utility, not evangelism. Utility means building rails that bitcoin and stablecoins can use together seamlessly, adding bitcoin to mainstream fintech apps, and building new financial applications on top of the bitcoin chain. Perhaps none of this will light the fireworks at the radicals’ victory party or replace T-bills as the base layer of global finance, but every user who discovers the unique utility of bitcoin is further evidence of its mainstream adoption.

What we have is a thriving technology that enables us to do miraculous new things, and it’s achieved an undeniable scale, such that it is now too big to fail. That’s fantastic. It may not be the future we were dreaming about seven years ago in Berlin, but it’s wonderful in its own right, and it’s worth cultivating and celebrating.

Even though nobody sets out to grow up and become boring one day, it’s still a valid kind of success. It means you’ve made it, and you’re doing fine. Boring is what happens when things just work and things have just worked out. So we didn’t break the world with bitcoin. Oh well. We’re making a new one. A party with adults present is still a party. And maybe we’re now the adults. So dance while you wait for the dollar to collapse 😉

More traders are betting on Solana’s price going up.

But in a bear market, the bigger question is: what are these traders actually betting on? Technically, SOL continues to slide, with its November losses now reaching 22%.

The key takeaway? SOL dropped as low as $64 this month, wiping out the gains from its Q2 rally, when it hit a local high of $125.

DEX volumes fell to $406 billion in Q4 from $667bn in Q3, according to DeFiLlama. Nonetheless, Solana continues to account for close to 23% of DEX volumes, highlighting that it still has moderately good trading volumes, despite the poor performance of its native token SOL.

Against this backdrop, the rise in Solana [SOL] long positions starts to make strategic sense.

High DEX trading volumes can drive significant transaction and space costs, which in turn can add further value to SOL. It can also increase revenue and offer market liquidity. T

raders may be betting that this sustained activity will eventually translate into stronger demand for SOL and support a price recovery.

Meanwhile, the SOL/BTC pair is also re-testing Q2 support, while BTC.D is nearing 60% resistance. Should it fail here, BTC.D may fall and funds may shift out of Bitcoin and into altcoins.

In doing so, Solana’s strong DEX data may prove fundamental. That said, the stakes couldn’t be higher.

Solana is heading for its worst year since inception.

Following a 20%+ correction in November, data from CoinGlass suggests that SOL looks set to end the month in negative territory. This would result in 9 out of 12 months being down for SOL in 2026. There were also 9 negative months for SOL in 2022. So, should December not reverse this trend, 2026 could even exceed this and prove to be Solana’s weakest year yet in terms of monthly performance.

Despite consistent month-on-month weakness, SOL’s annual ROI stands at -40%, slightly better than Ethereum’s -41%. It therefore appears that the issues facing Solana are not only those affecting the broader market but also relate specifically to the project.

Put simply, repeated monthly losses show how difficult it is for SOL bulls to hold support, leaving SOL susceptible to further downside.

According to AMBCrypto, this divergence could work against Solana.

The logic is simple: Strong DEX activity has yet to translate into buying pressure, while repeated monthly losses show that buyers are struggling to regain control. If this weakness continues, traders betting on a recovery could get caught on the wrong side. Leveraged liquidations could then add to selling pressure.

Thus, what looks like a recovery bet could quickly turn into a major bull trap.

Solana’s DEX activity remains strong, but its price continues to fall.

Rising long positions despite repeated monthly losses increase the risk of a bull trap and further liquidations.

Without a major psychological threshold, moving averages are the only benchmarks for us. The price has reached the 20-day moving average after violating $67 price level. Redeeming a matured pool share first unwinds the position and redeems the principal tokens it held, with the app showing which output is available and how much the holder would receive.

Holders who receive stXRP can swap stXRP at the market price, which can differ from Firelight’s vault value, or request a direct withdrawal.

The direct route stops rewards at the request and makes FXRP claimable in 30 to 60 days under Firelight’s current coverage schedule. A second transaction collects the FXRP, and eligible claims from periods the capital backed can still reduce the payout.

FXRP received from any of those routes is still on Flare, so getting XRP back on its own ledger takes a separate FAssets redemption.

On the standard route, Flare burns the FXRP, and an agent sends native XRP to the holder’s XRP Ledger address after fees by the payment deadline. A holder who redeems directly into FXRP can go straight to that step.

Holders already able to redeem into FXRP can request native XRP without taking on a new maturity or waiting through Firelight’s unstaking window. For holders leaving with stXRP, a market swap avoids the vault’s wait if a usable quote is available.

#5085. Bitcoin privacy weakness links wallet addresses to network nodes in 30 out of 30 tests

On Nov. 25, researcher Abubakar Sadiq Ismail reported linking addresses to the correct nodes in all 30 attempts in regtest, Bitcoin Core’s local testing environment.

Ismail said the same behavior can expose a watch-only wallet, which monitors addresses and transactions without storing the keys needed to spend the funds.

A service can keep its spending keys off the machine it uses to monitor deposits, and a match identifies the node whose wallet recognizes the address.

In his write-up on wallet rebroadcast for Delving Bitcoin, Ismail described a long-known behavior in Bitcoin Core. After a wallet learns about an unconfirmed transaction, it can announce that transaction again to peers.

That repeated announcement can reveal that the node’s wallet recognizes activity involving a particular address or output. The blockchain records confirmed transactions, while the extra clue about who tracks an address comes from the node’s network activity.

Ismail’s reported matches show that wallet behavior can reveal an address-to-node link in a controlled network.

A node is a computer running software that exchanges information with peers on the Bitcoin network. Its wallet tracks addresses and transactions, and software that loads addresses into a Bitcoin Core wallet can inherit the exposure, even when its role is limited to monitoring.

One node may track two addresses that belong to different users of the same service, and a single operator can also run several nodes. An observer who sees a match learns how a wallet is used, while ownership across those addresses remains uncertain.

Please enable JavaScript to verify and send this form.

A repeat announcement can connect a Bitcoin address to the node whose wallet tracks it.

Watch-only wallets hold no spending keys. An address-to-node match leaves spending control unknown.

This is a conceptual diagram of the reported Bitcoin Core wallet behavior. It gives no estimate of how often an observer could make an attribution on mainnet.

The solid line represents the tracking link described by Abubakar Sadiq Ismail on Delving Bitcoin. The open marker identifies the remaining question of who holds the spending keys.

This is a conceptual diagram of the reported Bitcoin Core wallet behavior. It gives no estimate of how often an observer could make an attribution on mainnet.

An operator can use private broadcast to shield the initial announcement of a transaction. If it stays unconfirmed, Bitcoin Core’s wallet may later announce it more broadly.

A user who chooses a private path for the first announcement can still lose some of that protection in the later broadcast.

Ismail pointed to -walletbroadcast=0 as a way to disable wallet-initiated announcements, which also stops the wallet from automatically announcing the user’s own new transactions. Users who turn off wallet broadcasting need a separate way to relay the payments they intend to send.

A pending Bitcoin Core proposal would preserve part of rebroadcast’s original purpose. A pending transaction can drop out of a node’s mempool, its local pool of unconfirmed transactions, and still need another chance to reach the network.

Bitcoin Core pull request #36482 would limit wallet rebroadcast to transactions the node newly accepts into that pool. The wallet could still relay transactions that had dropped out if the node accepts them again.

It would suppress repeat announcements for transactions already in a node’s mempool, while other wallet rebroadcasts could still reveal which node recognizes a transaction.

XRP is on track for its worst November on record and has lost 48.3% in 2026 so far. The token also ended 2014, 2018 and 2022 with annual losses.

CryptoRank data shows that XRP has lost 24% in November so far, as of Friday. Before 2026, the token's worst November was in 2019, when it lost 23.3%. The month will close on Monday, Nov. 30.

According to CryptoRank, XRP's high for 2026 was $2.40, and its low was $0.87 in November. In the fourth quarter, the token has lost 36.1% so far, and in 2026, XRP has lost value in seven of 11 months so far. Veteran trader Peter Brandt has also used the four-year cycle in his forecasts for Bitcoin. In April 2026, Brandt said that if the cycle holds, Bitcoin's next peak could come in September or October 2029 at $300,000 to $500,000.

In 2014, XRP lost 10.7% over the year, but the token gained 130.4% in November and 118.1% in December, according to CryptoRank.

In 2018, XRP lost 84.5% over the year. The token also lost 19.3% and 2.25% in November and December of that year, respectively. In 2022, the annual loss was 59.2%, and XRP lost 11.8% in November and 16.9% in December.

XRP's median December return is -4.07%, and its average December return is 63.1%, according to CryptoRank data. In December 2017, XRP gained 818.9%. The token closed December in the red in eight of the past 13 years, including December 2025, when it lost 14.8%.

XRP's largest December loss came in 2020. The token lost 66.5% that month, after the SEC sued Ripple on Dec. 22, 2020.

XRP ended 2015 with a 75.3% loss and 2019 with a 47.1% loss, according to CryptoRank. In 2023, the token gained 82.5%.

In the first quarter of 2015, XRP lost 68.2%. The token lost 12.8% in the first quarter of 2019 and gained 58.8% in the first quarter of 2023.

According to Ripple, lenders will deposit funds into a Single Asset Vault, and loan brokers will use that capital to issue loans and track repayments on the ledger.

On Friday, the LendingProtocolV1_1 amendment reached 29 of 35 validator votes, according to XRPScan. Its earliest activation date is Dec. 11 at 2:22 p.m. UTC, and its support has to stay above 80% until then.

#5081. Galaxy Withdraws Call That Bitcoin’s Bear Market Ended in June

Galaxy has withdrawn its October call that bitcoin’s bear market ended in June, saying the technical signal behind it failed after seven straight weeks of losses and that the bear market is “very likely not over.”

Alex Thorn, Galaxy’s head of firmwide research, laid out the reversal in a report published Wednesday and sent to clients a day earlier. “We withdraw our call that the bear market ended in June,” the report said. “The signal it rested on has failed.”

The firm’s Oct. 26 note had argued that bitcoin had entered an accumulation phase. Galaxy said at the time that a weekly close back below the 50-week moving average that was not regained within a month would invalidate its technical case.

That is what happened. Bitcoin closed the week ended Nov. 8 at $74,968, 0.7% below the 50-week average, after seven weekly closes above it. It then closed the week ended Nov. 15 below the 200-week average, which Galaxy has described as the floor of past bear markets.

The week ended Nov. 22 closed at $61,104, 17.9% below the 50-week average and 10.4% below the 200-week average of $68,159. Bitcoin traded below its July 1 intraday low on Nov. 20 and reached $55,100 on Nov. 21, but the June 30 closing low of $58,525 held on a daily basis through Nov. 22.

Galaxy now treats that level as the line to watch. A daily close below $58,525 would be “the start of a move to a materially lower low,” the report said, and the firm would not treat such a close as a buying signal by itself.

History is not kind to breaks like that. In the seven prior bear market cases where bitcoin closed below a low that had stood for at least 60 days, the eventual low was at least 17% lower, with a median of 52%. Applied to the June low, that works out to about $48,500 and $28,200.

Bitcoin briefly slumped below $57,500 on Wednesday morning as the Nasdaq sank, but it ended the day back above $60,000 and has not posted a daily close below $58,525. It traded near $60,800 on Thursday morning.

Galaxy said two readings of the market disagree. By the calendar, this bear is old: Nov. 22 was day 412 since the Oct. 6, 2025, record, longer than the 163 to 406 days from high to low in the four prior bear markets.

By depth, it looks unfinished. Bitcoin’s 53% decline compares with drops of 77% to 93% in earlier bears. It also has not closed a day below its realized price of $53,205, something every prior bear did for at least 140 days, and only two of the 13 bottom signals Galaxy tracks have been met.

“The clock says this bear is overdue to end, the depth says it has further to fall, and we do not believe the price record alone can settle which,” the report said.

Flows have not helped. Galaxy estimates U.S. spot bitcoin ETPs hold about 1.24 million BTC, 9.7% below their October 2025 peak, after shedding 71,339 BTC, or $4.95 billion, since Oct. 4. November is shaping up as a record month for ETF outflows.

Galaxy said the other three parts of its October thesis, covering positioning, fundamentals and sentiment, are stronger now than when it published. Its proprietary Bitcoin Fear & Greed Index fell to 5.2 on Nov. 21, its lowest reading since June 30, 2022.

To swing back toward its October view, Galaxy wants a weekly close above the 200-week average and then the 50-week average, now $74,401, with the June weekly closing low of $59,517 holding. A weekly close below realized price would point to a deeper bear.

“We are not trying to call the low,” the report said. “Until one gives way, we will judge the market on weekly closes rather than headlines.”

Chainflip finalized its user loss assessment following a $12.6 million exploit, laying the groundwork for a recovery fund.

Chainflip said on Nov. 27 that it had finished assessing how the theft from its Bitcoin and Ethereum vaults affected user balances.

The cross-chain swap protocol said the accounting gives it a basis to develop a recovery plan for people who were swapping at the time, regular account holders, and liquidity providers who supply assets for trades.

In its second incident report, Chainflip said it had finalized the list of affected users and the method for calculating the impact on each account. It said it will settle outstanding loans at prices from the time of the Nov. 21 attack to finalize affected balances.

The team said it could use the list to record the losses on-chain and set up a recovery fund managed by the protocol.

The new accounting looks at the impact on individual accounts, which is what Chainflip says will inform its recovery proposal.

Chainflip began returning free balances to liquidity providers on five unaffected networks while it assessed losses. The first report named Solana, Arbitrum, Tron, BNB Chain and Polkadot Asset Hub. Governance used designated refund addresses to send back those available funds.

The first report said assets in open loans, strategies, or range orders could still be held in Chainflip accounts, so a provider could receive a precautionary refund and still have assets in an open position.

Chainflip said the protocol remains paused pending security review and fixes. It said major active liquidity providers were willing to return if that work met a high standard and a plan to replenish their capital was put into effect.

Chainflip and the Crosschain Association are also working to add SwapKit to the existing swap site. That temporary service would route new trades through other providers while Chainflip works on its own restart.

Israel Discount Bank opened Bitcoin and Ethereum trading in its retail banking app on Nov. 26, letting eligible customers buy, hold, and sell the two assets through their securities account.

The service blocks transfers to private wallets and outside institutions. To cash out, customers sell in the app, and the bank credits US dollars to their account.

The bank’s product FAQ says the service is available to Israeli residents aged 18 and older who have signed up for securities trading with Discount Bank.

Customers then accept a separate crypto trading agreement in the app to place orders through the existing account and see the holdings alongside their other investments.

Customers who already hold Bitcoin or Ethereum elsewhere can’t bring those coins into the service, so the account serves as both the place to trade and the place where customers see their crypto holdings.

The bank credits sale proceeds in US dollars the next business day, and customers who want shekels or another currency can ask the bank to convert them.

Bitcoin and Ether stay inside the service. Customers sell in the app to receive dollars in their bank account.

Selling costs 2% before any currency conversion charge and credits U.S. dollars on the next business day.

#5072. Bitcoin Price Trades Near $61,300 as Tech Stock Futures Rally

The bitcoin price traded near $61,300 on Friday morning, as tech stock futures jumped ahead of a holiday-shortened session on Wall Street. Bitcoin price is on track for its first weekly gain after seven straight weekly losses, though it is still down about 20% in November.

The bitcoin price was up about 1.7% early Friday and set to add 4.8% for the week, Investing.com reported, extending a recovery from a two-year low of $57,325.70 hit earlier in the week. Bitcoin slumped below $57,500 on Wednesday as the Nasdaq sank at the open, before a late rebound in tech shares lifted risk assets.

Short sellers helped fuel the bounce. Shorts made up 77% of $84.7 million in bitcoin liquidations over the past day, while futures open interest was little changed. That suggests forced short covering, rather than fresh leverage, supplied much of the lift.

Nasdaq 100 futures rose 2.2% by 6:42 a.m. ET, Reuters reported, as investors returned from Thanksgiving and piled back into battered AI-linked shares. Nvidia gained 3.6% in premarket trading, while AMD climbed 4.4% and Broadcom added 3.4%. S&P 500 futures rose 1.6%, and Dow futures gained 1.3%.

“There have been some signs that the tech selloff has stabilised for now, and that risk appetite is returning to markets,” Deutsche Bank analysts said in a note cited by Reuters. The S&P 500 is headed for its best week since April, though it remains on course for its worst November since 2008.

Bitcoin price has followed that rebound but lagged it. The major U.S. stock indexes are each up around 4% on the week, and silver jumped about 7% to above $44 an ounce on Friday while gold added 2.5% to above $3,670. Stocks close early at 1 p.m. ET, and the bond market shuts at 2 p.m.

The macro backdrop still weighs on the bitcoin price. Traders are almost fully pricing in a Federal Reserve rate hike in December after data this week showed the economy grew faster than first estimated in the third quarter and inflation accelerated in October, Reuters reported. Third-quarter GDP growth was revised up to 4.3%, and the 10-year Treasury yield slipped to 4.84%.

Spot bitcoin ETFs are also still losing cash. The U.S. funds lost $453 million on Wednesday, their seventh straight day of outflows, with BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust accounting for $329.7 million. That pushed November outflows to about $5.39 billion, extending what was already a record month for the funds.

Crypto stocks face their own test in Friday’s short session. Strategy shares rose 3.1% to $79.96 on Wednesday, while Coinbase gained 1.3% to $103.72. Bitcoin miners that have moved into AI hosting tracked the tech rally, with IREN and Cipher Digital each gaining 8% in premarket trading.

Mining economics remain tight with the bitcoin price this low. CleanSpark has weighed selling more bitcoin than it mines after a $987 million loss, and network mining difficulty jumped 7.61% early Friday, reversing most of a 9.13% drop on Nov. 14. That means miners must spend more computing power for each bitcoin they earn.

On Nov. 26, Binance said it had lifted the withdrawal freeze imposed after its October hack, but customers moving crypto to their own wallets may still encounter pauses on individual networks or account restrictions.

Binance described those pauses as routine and separate from the work it did to restore withdrawals after the hack.

Open Binance’s withdrawal screen for the asset you want to send and check the status of the network you plan to use. You can also check that asset and network on Binance’s public network status page.

An asset may show an available withdrawal route while the account still has a hold. In that case, the status page answers the route question, and the notice on your account tells you what action Binance needs from you.

#5065. BNB Chain’s new blockchain could make the same PancakeSwap trade 27% more expensive

BNB Chain’s proposed gas rules would raise the network fee for a sample PancakeSwap trade by 27% at the same gas price.

On BNB Chain’s proposed network, a trader would pay for all the computing capacity a swap reserves. Applying that rule to one PancakeSwap trade on BNB Smart Chain would raise its network fee by about 27% at the same gas price.

BNB Chain published its new layer-1 litepaper on Nov. 26, describing a separate network being developed alongside BNB Smart Chain (BSC). The design keeps BNB as the gas token, and a public testnet is in preparation.

For trading apps, the proposal pairs early feedback about where a transaction might land with reserved capacity for eligible activity. The devnet bills ordinary transactions for the room they request in a block.

A gas limit is the maximum amount of computing work a transaction can use. On BNB Smart Chain, the network fee for an ordinary transaction reflects the gas it actually uses.

The new devnet orders transactions before execution, using the declared limit to allocate room in the block. An ordinary transaction with a valid sequence number and sufficient funds at execution pays for that full amount, even if it finishes with gas to spare.

On June 26, a successful swap through PancakeSwap’s v3 router used 129,397 gas at 0.05 gwei per unit and paid 0.00000646985 BNB.

At the same price and the same 163,957-gas limit, the new devnet rule would charge 0.00000819785 BNB. The 34,560 units of unused capacity would add 0.000001728 BNB to that one swap’s fee.

At a 150,000-gas limit, the modeled fee would be 0.0000075 BNB, about 16% above the observed BSC fee. At 200,000 gas, it would be 0.00001 BNB, about 55% higher. A router that lowers its limit can save on transactions that fit and still run out of gas when a route takes more work than expected.

A recorded PancakeSwap transaction and the proposed fee rule at the same gas price.

The swap’s recorded limit becomes the billed amount in the model.

Illustrative lower limit, with the original swap’s gas price held constant.

Illustrative higher limit, with the original swap’s gas price held constant.

The proposed rule bills unused gas, so increasing the limit raises the fee even when the swap uses the same amount of gas.

One historical swap. The model holds the effective gas price fixed and applies devnet billing to three declared limits. The alternatives do not establish future network prices or successful execution at those limits.

The June 26, 2026 BSC receipt shows 129,397 gas used and a 163,957 limit at 0.05 gwei. Apply 0.05 gwei to the selected declared limit in the new L1 model. Divide each modeled fee difference by the observed fee and round to the nearest whole percent. Bars show billed gas on a shared 200,000-gas scale.

One historical swap. The model holds the effective gas price fixed and applies devnet billing to three declared limits. The alternatives do not establish future network prices or successful execution at those limits.

An included transaction that meets those conditions still pays the full limit if it reverts or runs out of gas under the devnet fee rules. At execution, an invalid transaction sequence number incurs no gas charge, while insufficient funds can limit what the network collects.

Please enable JavaScript to verify and send this form.

The network’s protected lanes reserve a portion of block capacity for transactions sent to governance-approved contract addresses. A swap sent to an unregistered router cannot use the reservation of a contract that the router calls.

The declared limit counts against a lane’s quota, so a larger buffer also leaves less room for other eligible transactions. Eligible transactions still compete for space within a lane.

The devnet’s preconfirmation documentation lists roughly 20 milliseconds for the block producer to stream a signed update showing a transaction’s intended position.

The transaction’s result is final after execution is committed and the block carrying that commitment has finalized. An app settling a trade needs a successful receipt and must confirm the receipt’s block is on the canonical chain and at or below the execution-finalized height.

A market maker might delay a quote update after seeing that a swap likely to change its reference price has provisional placement.

If the signal prevents costly stale quotes often enough, those savings can cover the recurring charge for unused gas. If the signal is withdrawn, the market maker has to reassess. A router that needs a swap outcome before making its next move still has to wait for execution.

BNB Smart Chain recorded $484.13 million in 24-hour decentralized exchange volume in DefiLlama’s Nov. 27 snapshot.

For any of that activity to move, the proposed network would have to make economic sense for traders at real gas prices. Public testing can show which lanes are available, how often placement signals are withdrawn, and how much spare gas different routes need.

#5060. Bitcoin miners hit by hashrate hijacking attack exploiting unencrypted connections

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Braiins is urging miners to upgrade to Stratum V2 to encrypt their connections.

Bitcoin mining pool Braiins uncovered a widespread attack that redirects bitcoin miners' hash power to steal their rewards, which it says is still ongoing.

Braiins detailed how the attack works in a Wednesday report. Bad actors are said to be exploiting a weakness in Stratum V1, a protocol used by many bitcoin miners to communicate with mining pools.

The attackers are impersonating mining pools by rerouting internet traffic, making it so miners' hashrate is being hijacked by imposters while it looks like they are mining as usual. Meanwhile, the rewards that would have been earned by the miners are instead flowing into wallets controlled by the hijackers.

Braiins identified several waves of attacks throughout November, first cropping up in Latin America before spreading to Europe. The amount of computing power being targeted grew exponentially over the span of a couple of weeks.

"The episodes so far were short, but they grew from 175 PH/s to 1.9 EH/s in two weeks, the attacker changed the method between the two waves, and it moved from one continent to another," Braiins said. "We interpret this as testing the waters."

The vulnerability has reportedly been known about for more than a decade. Braiins pointed to a 2014 incident that was originally documented by Dell SecureWorks, where an attacker used the technique to steal around $83,000 in bitcoin and other proof-of-work mining rewards over four months.

Braiins said its own systems were not compromised and that its mining pool accounts, balances and payouts were unaffected. It did not provide an estimate of the mining rewards stolen in the latest attack. It urged miners to switch to encrypted connections and the newer Stratum V2 protocol to protect themselves and their customers.

#5059. Spain Lets Anti-Money Laundering Unit Freeze Crypto Accounts Without a Judge

Spain has given its financial intelligence unit the power to freeze crypto accounts on its own authority, without first getting a judge’s approval, when it suspects money laundering or terrorist financing.

The change was published in Spain’s official state gazette on Wednesday as part of Royal Decree-Law 44/2026, a sweeping decree that mostly deals with consumer credit contracts and the sale of bad loan portfolios. Its sixth final provision adds a new Article 46 bis to the country’s 2010 anti-money laundering law.

The new article lets the Executive Service of the Commission for the Prevention of Money Laundering and Monetary Offenses, known as Sepblac, suspend or refuse to authorize a transaction in progress. It can also suspend the use of a bank, payment or crypto-asset account, or a business relationship, when there are “indications” that it could be tied to money laundering or terrorist financing.

According to the text, the goal is to preserve the funds while Sepblac carries out its analysis and checks whether the suspicion holds up. If it does, the unit passes the information to the competent authorities so they can take further action.

The decree sets two separate time limits. Sepblac can hold a pending transaction for no more than 10 business days, and it can freeze an account or business relationship for no more than five. Either hold must be lifted sooner if it is no longer needed to preserve the funds.

When the suspicion comes from a suspicious activity report filed by a bank or other regulated firm, Sepblac must issue the suspension within three business days of that report. When the case comes from the unit’s own analysis, the decree says it must act “as soon as possible.”

Once those deadlines pass, the freeze ends unless a court ratifies or extends it at the request of the public prosecutor’s office. Appeals against a court’s decision follow Spain’s criminal procedure law.

The decree also shields Sepblac, its staff and the firms that carry out its orders from liability. Firms that ignore a suspension order commit an offense under the anti-money laundering law. Sepblac can also act at the request of Spanish police and security forces, or of financial intelligence units in other EU states and outside the bloc.

Until now, Sepblac could only use this power when a foreign financial intelligence unit asked it to. The government said in the decree’s preamble that the limit is a deficiency the Financial Action Task Force will assess, and that waiting longer could hurt Spain’s international evaluation.

The government also said the speed of financial transactions, especially online, lets possibly criminal funds move before authorities can finish their analysis. The provision transposes Article 24 of an EU directive adopted in May 2024 on the mechanisms member states must set up to fight money laundering.

The rule takes effect Jan. 25, 2027, two months after the decree’s publication. As a royal decree-law, it must also be put to a vote in Spain’s Congress of Deputies within 30 days to be validated or repealed.

The decree does not name individual crypto platforms, and it is not yet clear how exchanges operating in Spain will receive and carry out the orders. Several European governments have been moving the same way. Poland’s parliament voted 240-202 this month to let officials freeze bitcoin and bank funds of people on a national sanctions list before a court reviews the case.

Other moves in Europe have gone the opposite way. France’s Senate rejected amendments that would have forced holders to declare self-custody wallets worth €100,000 or more, while Binance is closing accounts in four EU countries at the end of the year.

Under the decree, crypto-asset accounts fall under the same five-day freeze limit as bank and payment accounts.

#5056. Your Guide to Running on the Treadmill This Winter

Here’s why it feels harder to run indoors—and how to hack it to make it more enjoyable.

There’s almost no other cardio machine that brings up as many feelings as the treadmill. For the first few years of my running career, I’d do just about everything I could to avoid hopping on one, even if that meant running in freezing temps or heavy rain.

Then, last winter happened. There was more snow and ice on the ground in New York City than I had seen in a long time, but I had a half-marathon to train for. It left me no choice: I had to move my workouts to the treadmill unless I wanted to end up like that meme where the woman says snow is the perfect texture for running just to wipe out on live television a few seconds later.

But, as any treadmill hater knows, moving a run indoors isn’t as simple as it sounds. A lot changes on a tread—form, mental stimulation, pace—and it can totally mess with your head. Once you understand why, though, it’s a lot easier to work with the treadmill instead of against it; here’s how.

Because it is! For starters, your form changes. “Many people shorten their stride on the treadmill—me included,” says Amy Woods, a USAT-certified run coach and ISSA-certified strength and conditioning coach. “We also tend to run a little more upright.”

There’s a simple reason behind it. When you’re running outside, your legs have all the space they need for each stride, but on a treadmill, you’re contained to the length and width of the belt. Plus, most people tend to stick too close to the front of the tread, making their space even smaller, says Morgan Mowers, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and V.02-certified run coach.

Between a shortened stride and the fact that it’s a bit easier to propel yourself forward when you’ve got the help of the moving belt, you end up using different muscles on a treadmill compared to outdoors. “We see a decrease in activation of hamstrings and glutes, those bigger propellers that push you forward,” Mowers says. Instead, you’re seeing more activation in your hip flexors, quads, calves, and knees.

On paper, a lot of these differences should actually make treadmill running easier than running outside. Another example? A treadmill provides a consistent surface. Outside, terrain and incline can vary with each step, so you call on more stabilizing muscles in your ankles and calves, Mowers says. “With every step, there's a little bit of a change when you're running outside versus on a treadmill,” she says. “Even if you are changing up the incline, it's the same exact surface over and over again.” You also don’t have to deal with the same environmental challenges—like heat and wind resistance—that come with running outside. There’s even a famous 1996 study that claims runners should set their incline to 1 percent to accommodate for the difference.

Even with all these easier-sounding differences, running on a treadmill often feels anything but. For many people, myself included, slowing down on a treadmill is the norm. One possible reason: You may just not be used to it, Woods says. Running safely on a treadmill, especially at higher speeds, takes practice. “It's definitely a different feeling when you're running on a treadmill,” Woods says. “You have to be more aware of your foot placement, your arm swing, and where your eyes are looking.” Even if you’re not consciously aware of it, your proprioception (your ability to sense your body’s position in space) could be affected.

Plus, when you’re on the treadmill, you’re stuck at one pace unless you change it, Mowers points out. “That consistency that your body is feeling on a treadmill can make it feel harder, and also may result in you going at an overall slower pace,” she says. When you hop on a treadmill, you start yourself at a pace and settle in until you physically change it. Over the course of a mile outdoors, in comparison, you may start at an 11:00 pace, then speed up to a 10:45 pace for most of it, and end up cruising at a 10:30 pace—all without really noticing. Even though your effort feels the same, your outdoor mile ends up faster.

Then there’s the mental side of things. Outside, you’ve got much more stimulation, says Rachelle Reed, PhD, an exercise physiologist. Your surroundings can offer the perfect distraction, and the natural variations in scenery, incline, terrain, and pace can help keep your brain more engaged too. This can have an impact on your rate of perceived exertion (RPE), Reed says. In fact, a 2019 meta-analysis found that at faster speeds, runners rated their effort as harder on a treadmill compared to outdoors. Basically, it’s harder to go hard on the tread. And because running on a treadmill is technically easier than running outdoors because you have less variation, wind resistance, and environmental factors to navigate at any given moment, that higher RPE really speaks to the mental effects of being inside, Reed says.

The good news? All these differences between treadmill and outdoor running only really matter if you’re training for a race. That’s because come race day, you’ll want your muscles fully prepped to accommodate your outdoor stride, along with the ability to run across inconsistent terrain and in various elements, Mowers says. Meanwhile, if you’re just looking to do cardio, you can take your pick between the two.

If you are in fact training for a race, how should a treadmill fit into your training? In this case, going outside tends to be superior to staying in, our experts agree. Don’t move your run to the tread at just any sign of inconvenience—running in the rain, cold, and (reasonable) heat all make you a better runner, and you never know if those conditions will pop up on race day, so you’ll be glad to have the practice.

Still, there are definitely situations where it’s not a good idea to go outside. Mowers draws the line when it comes to safety: If the ground is icy, snowy, or slippery in any way, she’ll stay inside to avoid potential injury. If temps are dangerously hot, she’ll run on the treadmill. If there’s risk from serious weather, like thunder and lightning or flooding, she’ll also stay safe indoors. And, she’ll stick to her tread in the event of poor air quality (anything that’s an air quality index over 101).

It’s always worth considering personal safety, too. If your only window to run is late at night and you feel more comfortable staying indoors, do that.

How hot is too hot? This is going to vary down to the person and place. Anything above 85 degrees can be dangerous, Woods says, and you also need to factor in dew point, humidity, and the effort of your run. (Harder efforts are more risky than easier ones.) If temps are higher and you decide to run outdoors, make sure you bring plenty of hydration and fuel, go slower than normal, and pay attention to signs of overheating.

There’s also the convenience factor. You may need to do a run on the treadmill because it’s more accommodating to your schedule or childcare needs. That’s totally okay too. Ideally, the majority of your runs (we’re talking about 80 percent, and especially your long runs) will be outside, but if you’re someone who finds themselves needing to do the bulk of their running indoors, a run coach can help you make sure you’re prepped for race day. (Woods works with athletes who do the bulk of their training on treads—it’s possible!) The treadmill exists for a reason, and your training will not be affected by the occasional indoor run.

First and foremost, don’t be too hard on yourself about pace. “I always disconnect from pace on the treadmill,” Woods says. Instead, she focuses on her time and RPE. It’s really about thinking about the “spirit of the workout,” she says. For example, you can pay attention to what heart rate zone or effort level you’re supposed to get to and match that—even if that looks slower and feels harder indoors.

And, no, you don’t need to set your incline to 1 percent to compensate for bringing your workout indoors, our experts agree. The biggest reason? The study that established the idea was very small (it had just nine participants) and done only in men. That said, the incline buttons will become useful depending on the kind of run you have on deck for the day.

Finally, give yourself a good warm-up on the treadmill, Mowers says. “Just the act of getting on a treadmill is going to increase our heart rate a little bit because we're a hamster on a wheel; we're trying not to fall off of this thing, and we're so aware of the fact that we're running,” she says. You may need at least 10 to 15 minutes to settle in before getting started with the rest of your workout.

Here’s how to approach different kinds of runs indoors.

Nothing really has to change, Woods says. It may take you a little longer to run a 5K on your treadmill, but try to stick to the appropriate lower heart rate zones and RPE that you’d normally achieve on these kinds of runs outdoors.

You can play with incline if you’d like—but it’s not a requirement if this is a one-off run you’re doing inside. Running for one day on a completely flat surface won’t affect your training. One reason you may want to try changing the incline may simply be because it adds some variety and stimulation, Woods says. If you’re someone who struggles because the treadmill feels boring, try increasing the incline anywhere from 1 to 4 percent for anywhere from 30 seconds to a few minutes every so often.

Another hack: Every 10 minutes, increase your speed slightly. That should give you enough time to warm up a little each time and settle into the pace, so you shouldn’t see much of a jump in demand on your heart rate or effort.

This one gets a bit trickier, Woods says. Going at all-out speeds on a treadmill can be much tougher—and not feel super safe. This is a time when you’ll want to think about the spirit of the workout. If you have intervals where you’re supposed to get to max heart rate efforts, instead of turning up the speed super high, you can increase the incline in addition to adjusting the speed slightly, Woods says. That should still get you to your zone 4 or 5, all while allowing you to stay slower and feel more in control. This is much easier to accomplish in a tempo run (where you’re holding the pace for longer chunks of time) compared to intervals, so you could also swap an interval run for tempo too.

You also have the option to skip a speed workout, Woods says. Missing one session won’t have an impact on your training, and if you’d rather not do it on the treadmill, you also have the option to switch it with another run for the week.

Now, here’s a workout that translates pretty well to the treadmill: All you have to do is up your incline for the duration marked in your workout. Woods recommends sticking between 1 and 4 percent as a good rule of thumb, but you can always bump up to 5 to 8 as long as you can keep good run form.

Ideally, you can move your long run to another day when you can run outside. But, if not, go by time—not mileage. Woods doesn’t recommend running on a treadmill for longer than two hours unless you are very experienced on one because of how it affects your form.

You also have the option to break up your run and do 90 minutes in the morning and 90 minutes in the afternoon. “This will help with form deterioration which is more noticeable and can be more dangerous on a tread,” Woods says.

While you’re on your long run, you’ll also want to incorporate moments of incline running and even some pace variation—both for improving your running and also giving yourself a mental reset. Woods also loves to sprinkle in 15- to 30-second walking breaks every mile or so to reset her form and hydrate.

Then the world is really your oyster on the treadmill, but all the same ideas apply: Focus on time and effort, not pace. And, feel free to sprinkle in different inclines and speeds to work different heart rate zones and find moments of mental reset.

#5054. Sens. Warren, Van Hollen lead push to scrap SEC’s Regulation Crypto and innovation exemption

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

In a letter sent to SEC Chair Atkins, Sens. Warren and Van Hollen said the agency's "Regulation Crypto Assets" would allow crypto firms to circumvent securities laws.

Top Democrats Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Chris Van Hollen are demanding that Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Paul Atkins take down its crypto rulemaking governing how crypto projects can raise capital and how tokenized securities can be traded.

In two separate letters sent to Atkins on Tuesday, Sens. Warren, Van Hollen and Tina Smith and other Senate Banking Committee members said the agency's "Regulation Crypto Assets" would allow crypto firms to circumvent securities laws, weaken state jurisdiction and could harm investors.

"The proposal would create a new 'tailored securities offering regime' for certain investment contracts involving crypto assets," the senators wrote. "However, the proposal only serves to help crypto assets escape from the SEC's regulatory regime and gives them special treatment—with less oversight—compared to other traditional securities."

In August, the SEC proposed crypto offering rules to offer startup and fundraising exemptions for digital asset offerings. It allows for a "startup exemption" that would exempt offerings of up to $5 million from registration rules under the Securities Act of 1933 for four years — a federal law focused on anti-fraud and requiring certain disclosures. The proposal also includes a "fundraising exemption" for offerings up to $75 million for a year.

Warren is poised to take on a more prominent role following Democrats’ victories in November's midterm elections, which handed the party control of both chambers of Congress. Warren has been critical of crypto in the past and has particularly brought up concerns around illicit finance and money laundering. Meanwhile, Van Hollen could be the next Senate Majority Leader. He has since challenged current Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer for that role.

Sens. Jack Reed and Tina Smith join the two in the second letter asking the SEC to withdraw its innovation exemption — a measure released in September to bring capital markets onchain through the trading of tokenized stocks. It is a five-year exemption that would exempt certain trading venues, called tokenized securities venues, from being defined as an exchange and also exempts specific liquidity providers from being defined as a dealer under securities law when they trade stocks or provide liquidity through automated market makers.

The senators said it would allow platforms to operate outside of certain safeguards, including involving fair pricing and market transparency.

"The order would allow TSV platforms to operate a shadow stock market outside longstanding regulatory protections designed to ensure fair and transparent markets, impose new burdens on publicly traded companies seeking to protect their shareholders, and create unnecessary risks of illicit financial activity," the senators wrote.

The three senators also said the innovation exemption could cause capital markets to splinter.

"As concerned stakeholders have pointed out, fragmenting our securities markets by creating a lightly regulated alternative marketplace for tokenized securities unnecessarily risks dividing liquidity into isolated pools and expanding opportunities for corrosive regulatory arbitrage," they said.

A separate group of Senate Democrats have also brought up concerns about the innovation exemption. Last week, Sens. Angela Alsobrooks, Ruben Gallego, Mark Warner and Catherine Cortez Masto said it could open the door for illicit finance actors and also had concerns about protections for retail investors around pricing.

#5052. The 8 Best Standing Desks for Walking Pads, Tested and Reviewed

From budget picks to tricked-out options for a better WFH space.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

You log a lot of time at your desk, making it fair to wonder how to create a workspace that’s as comfortable and healthy for you as possible. If sitting on your butt all day isn’t your idea of a good time, it makes sense to consider investing in a walking pad. To create a seamless workspace, you’ll need a special desk to go with that. The best standing desks for walking pads allow you to cruise along as you work, while still providing all the usual trappings you expect from a desk.

While TikTok is packed with happy-looking people working this way, the treadmill desk is more than a trend. Research ties sitting all day with a higher risk of developing back pain and even issues with cardiovascular health, making it a good idea to try to get up and move as much as possible during your day.

“Prolonged sitting has been linked to a number of health concerns, which is why many people are turning to standing desks,” says Andrew J. Bach, DO, a physiatrist at Cedars-Sinai Spine Center in Los Angeles “A standing desk allows you to get your usual computer-based work done while on your feet, and it comes with several benefits over sitting all day.” (He lists off better circulation, less strain on your back, more calories burned, and better digestion as just a few.)

But proper form is critical with these. “People should keep in mind how long they have been in a certain position, and their posture specifically,” says Meg Darmofal, DPT, a physical therapist at Michigan State University. You don’t want to shrug your shoulders, reach too far forward, bend over, or crane your neck up or down to see your screen, she says—all of those can put you at risk for developing aches and pains.

To find the best standing desks for walking pads, we consulted experts and had Women's Health editors test several popular models in their own workspaces. Our top pick is the Uplift Standing Desk V3, thanks to its easy height adjustments, customizable design, and compatibility with a walking pad. Ahead, find our favorite options for different budgets, spaces, and work-from-home setups.

While everyone has different needs in a standing desk, the Uplift V3 is packed with enough features and adjustability to make it a good fit for most. This motorized desk has a height range of 22.6 to 48.7 inches and comes in a wide range of tabletop widths and desktop styles, giving you plenty to choose from.

The desk has an impressive 355-pound lifting capacity, so you can pile a lot on it. WH copyeditor Deanna Martin tested the V3 alongside a walking pad and loved how easily the setup transformed her home office. The desk moves up and down with the touch of a keypad, making it easy to switch between sitting, standing, and walking throughout the workday.

Martin also liked the customizable accessories, which include storage options and even a hammock. There's also a companion app that tracks your standing progress and estimated calorie burn, though you'll need a Bluetooth adapter to connect it to the desk. Best of all, she found the entire setup super easy to assemble.

At over $600, the V3 is certainly an investment. But its versatile design, smooth height adjustments, and 15-year warranty are worth the price point.

It’s fair to expect to pay more for a motorized standing desk, but this Flexispot option manages to deliver that important feature with a relatively low price tag. The desk moves between 28 and 47.6 inches, giving you plenty to work with. It also has four height presets operated by an LED control panel, and a relatively roomy desktop space.

The desk includes a hook for your headphones or bag, allowing you to keep them in close reach while you work. It also can handle 176 pounds of weight, which should be plenty to work with. While it doesn’t have as many features as pricier desks like the Uplift 3, it’s still a solid, sturdy option to support you through your workday and comes much more affordably.

Whether you already have a desk you like or just don’t want to splash out for a totally new model, a standing desk converter can be a good middle ground. This option from Rocelco simply plops on top of your existing table to create a standing desk, so you can use a walking pad without replacing your entire WFH setup.

While some standing desk converters are small, this one can hold up to two large monitors, a laptop, and more. There’s a retractable keyboard tray, although it may not extend far enough for everyone's needs. The height adjustment is manual, but easy to do with the turn of a dial. There’s even a grommet hole to help you organize your cords, giving you a lot of the perks of a standing desk without the full commitment. Just make sure your existing desk and converter are tall enough to accommodate your walking pad.

A contoured standing desk allows you to get in close to your workspace, with an ergonomic design that can help you maintain a comfortable position while walking on a treadmill. This Fully Jarvis desk is sleek and comfortable, with a gently sloping and curved front that feels natural under your arms.

During testing, we were able to put this desk together quickly. It has a very sturdy feel, which is helpful when you’re walking while using it. The desk also thoughtfully includes an outlet and USB/lightning charger, so you can plug in your computer without having to bend over. The motor adjusts easily, although it can be a little choppy when you move up and down. Overall, we found that it was easy and comfortable to use. It looks and feels like a high-quality desk thanks to its bamboo surface and sturdy steel frame, making this a workspace you’ll use for years.

Having a little extra storage space can go a long way when you're trying to keep your home office organized. This Sanodesk standing desk features built-in drawers to stash away your office clutter. It's also motorized, so you can easily adjust the height when you want to sit, stand, or hop on your walking pad.

WH Designer Taryn Colbert tested the desk for two weeks and gave it a four out of five. She liked its spacious, easy-to-clean surface and preset heights. “It’s perfect,” she says, adding that it was “easy to put together for a person thats not very handy.”

Her biggest gripes? She wished the power plug were positioned farther toward the back of the desk, rather than toward the front and side, and would have preferred a long, slim drawer for additional storage.

This electric standing desk from Veken has a compact design that won't take over your home office, along with a motorized height adjustment system that makes it easy to switch between sitting and standing. There are also programmable height presets, so you don't have to find your preferred position every time.

WH Fitness Editor Cori Ritchey tested the desk for two to four weeks and gave it a five out of five. She was super impressed by how sturdy it felt, even when raised to its maximum height. “It feels well made for a desk that the buyer assembles (no shaky IKEA feeling here, even when at its max height!),” she says. Ritchey also liked the easy-to-use height adjustments and wide range of positions.

Her biggest gripe was the size. While the 36-inch desktop was great for occasional use, she wished she'd gone up a size for everyday work. She also found the textured surface a little tricky to clean after spills.

This walking pad features a removable desktop that attaches to the treadmill's railings, giving you a convenient spot for your laptop or tablet while you clock your steps. WH Lifestyle Director Lindsay Geller tested the setup for over a month and gave it a five out of five. She especially liked how sturdy the desktop felt once attached and how easy it was to remove. “This is a really great way to get a second desk without actually committing to buying a full desk,” she says, noting that she shares a home office with her husband. She also found assembly straightforward, putting the entire setup together by herself in about an hour.

The desk is admittedly basic, and the treadmill doesn't offer adjustable incline. Geller also found the walking surface a little narrow for jogging, making this a better option for walking while working than more intense workouts.

Every standing desk has either a set height or height range. Bach points out that height is a “key factor” in your desk. “If you’re especially tall or short, make sure the desk can adjust to a level that works for you,” he says. Just keep in mind that you’ll want to include the height of your walking pad when figuring out the right standing desk height for you, since you’ll be on top of it while you use your desk. “Returning a bulky standing desk can be a hassle, so it’s best to get the right fit from the start,” Bach says. Ideally, your desk should be high enough that you can type comfortably while standing on your walking pad, without having to hunch over or raise your shoulders.

Not all standing desks are adjustable, but many are—and it’s a nice feature to have. “Being able to easily lower and raise the desk is important because, in some scenarios, returning to sitting is good as well,” Darmofal says. Some desks can be heavy and awkward to move manually, which can be frustrating if you plan to switch between sitting and standing during the day, Bach says. “Motorized options are the most convenient, since they transition with the push of a button,” he adds. (Just keep in mind that motorized options tend to cost more.)

At the end of the day, this is still a desk, and you need one that will hold your stuff. Make sure you factor in space to hold your computer, pens, notepad, water bottle, and anything else you usually have on your desk. If you're using a walking pad, you'll also want enough room for your keyboard and monitor so you don't have to lean forward while walking.

It’s important to make sure that your desk’s legs and any footing are wide enough to leave space for your walking pad to slip between. Pay close attention to the walking pad dimensions and desk dimensions, leaving a little room around the pad so you’re not jamming it in there.

We should also note that a lot of our standing desk selections below don't come with a walking pad (though the Sharper Image Treadmill Desk is an all-in-one option), meaning it's an additional expense. If you don't already have one, make sure to check out our under-desk treadmill buying guide.

I consulted with Bach and Darmofal to help identify what to look for in standing desks for walking pads. From there, I researched top models, narrowing the field based on criteria like comfort, adjustability, and ease of use. Because everyone has a different experience, I also paid close attention to customer reviews and prioritized desks with overwhelmingly positive feedback.

From there, Women's Health editors put several standing desks to the test in their own workspaces. Our testers included Cori Ritchey, Lindsay Geller, Taryn Colbert, and Deanna Martin, who evaluated the desks for build quality, ease of assembly, adjustability, size, and overall functionality. Testing periods ranged from one week to over a month, with editors using their desks while sitting, standing, or walking on an under-desk treadmill. We also considered how stable each setup felt, how easily it fit into a home office, and any drawbacks our testers encountered.
